title: Predictive Maintenance Business Case: How to Build One
summary: Build a predictive maintenance business case finance can check: four lines, priced benefit buckets, a conservative avoidable share and a payback period.
body_markdown:
## Key Points


- A case finance approves has four lines: today's exposure, the share you can avoid, the cost of the fix and the payback period.
- Benefits go in separate buckets (production, labor and parts, risk) so finance can check each one.
- In an independent Verdantix study, three in four savings events in the paper industry were worth more than $5,000 each.


Before finance funds predictive maintenance, it usually wants the problem named, tied to specific assets and priced: what[unplanned downtime](https://tractian.com/en/glossary/unplanned-downtime) cost your plant over the last 12 months. Once that number is agreed, finance wants to know what happens next. If they fund a fix, how much of that cost goes away, what does it cost, and when does it pay back?


That's the job of a[predictive maintenance](https://tractian.com/en/glossary/predictive-maintenance) business case. It can be short, as long as every line traces back to a number finance can verify, a source they can read, or an assumption you've stated out loud.


## What does finance need to see in a predictive maintenance business case?


Finance needs four lines:


1. **Today's exposure:** what the problem costs you now, per year.
2. **The share you can avoid:** how much of that cost a predictive approach can realistically prevent.
3. **The cost of the fix:** what it takes to implement and run, over the period you're measuring.
4. **The payback period:** how long until the avoided cost covers the cost of the fix.


Today's exposure is already written. Start with the problem statement: the assets, the number of unplanned events, the hours lost, the cost per hour and the emergency premium. Finance has seen it, and if they've agreed it's real, you don't need to argue it again.


The other three are where most cases go wrong. Some teams skip the avoidable share and claim the whole exposure, which finance knows is unrealistic. Others bundle every benefit into one large number that nobody can check. The rest of this piece walks through each one so it holds up when finance takes it apart.


## Which predictive maintenance benefits can you put a number on?


Put each benefit in its own bucket, so finance can check each one against its own source. Three predictive maintenance benefits can usually be priced with data you already have.


- **Avoided downtime (production).** When a failure is caught early, the repair happens during a planned stop instead of halting the line. The value is the downtime hours you avoid multiplied by your cost per hour. This is usually the largest bucket, and it comes straight from today's exposure.
- **Avoided repair labor and parts.** A planned repair costs less than an emergency one. You avoid overtime, rush shipping, premium-priced parts and contractor call-outs. Your[work orders](https://tractian.com/en/glossary/work-order) and invoices from the last 12 months show what emergencies actually cost you compared with planned work.
- **Avoided secondary damage.** A bearing replaced on schedule is one part. A bearing that[runs to failure](https://tractian.com/en/glossary/run-to-failure-rtf) can take a shaft, a coupling or a motor with it. Use your own failure history where you can: look at past failures where the repair went well beyond the original defect.
- **Risk (safety, compliance, quality)** belongs in the case too, but list it separately and don't force it into dollars. A failure that puts a technician near a running machine, triggers a compliance finding or sends bad product to a customer matters to leadership. But a made-up dollar figure for it is the fastest way to lose finance's trust in every other number on the page. Describe the risk, name the assets involved, and let it strengthen the case without padding the total.


## What is a caught failure worth?


It depends on the sector, and the spread is wide. In a study Tractian commissioned from[Verdantix](https://tractian.com/en/resources/reports/verdantix) , an independent research firm, the value of each savings event (a failure caught before it caused unplanned downtime) varied a lot by industry (Verdantix study for Tractian, Figure 8):


Sector Savings events above US$5,000 Notable band


Paper 75%


Plastic 64%


Wood 60% 18% above $100,000


Oil and gas 56%


Maritime 58% between $20K and $100K; 15% above $100K


Beverage 54% between $1K and $5K


In paper, 75% of savings events were worth more than $5,000 each, while in beverage more than half fell between $1,000 and $5,000. The method is the same in both sectors, but the value per catch is very different. Use the row closest to your plant to sanity-check your own numbers, not to replace them.


At[Ingredion](https://tractian.com/en/case-studies/ingredion) , a DSM pump with no backup had a known history of 3-day outages. When a looseness defect was detected on it, a work order went out right away and a costly shutdown was avoided.


At[Tate & Lyle's San Diego facility](https://tractian.com/en/case-studies/cpkelco) , where a failure on the fermenter agitators could stop production for 3 to 4 days, the team recorded $446.9K in total cost savings within months, including $380K in production uptime and 84 hours of downtime avoided.


Different[failure modes](https://tractian.com/en/glossary/failure-mode) show up in different signals. Looseness and unbalance show in vibration, while rotor, stator and winding faults are electrical. A wider view of each failure mode gives the avoidable share in your case firmer footing.


Tractian[multimodal monitoring](https://tractian.com/en/solutions/multimodal) combines mechanical monitoring from Smart Trac Ultra, mounted on the asset, with electrical monitoring from[Energy Trac](https://tractian.com/en/solutions/energy-trac) , installed in the electrical panel that feeds the motor. Smart Trac Ultra is[Class I Div 1 ATEX/IECEx/NFPA compliant](https://tractian.com/en/solutions/sensor-specifications) . Janus, Tractian's industrial AI, correlates those signals with operational data, maintenance history and technical context to narrow down likely causes.


Tractian sensors install in a day with no cabling and no dependency on plant WiFi, and Tractian connects to[CMMS platforms](https://tractian.com/en/solutions/integrations) such as MaintainX, Fiix, UpKeep and Limble and to ERPs such as SAP and Oracle NetSuite.


## How do you estimate the share you can avoid?


Start from the 12 months of events in your problem statement and keep only the failures that give warning signs a monitoring system can pick up. Then apply a share you can defend, and write down why you chose it. That gives finance a number it can check.


- **Count only failures that give warning signs.** Go through the list event by event. A bearing that wore out over weeks, a misalignment that got worse, a motor that ran hot before it tripped: these leave a trail a sensor can read. A failure from operator error, a sudden electrical fault or a foreign object in the line usually doesn't. Take those out. What's left is the pool of failures predictive maintenance could plausibly have caught.
- **Keep the share conservative and say why.** Even among failures that give warning, not every one will be caught in time, and not every catch will lead to a planned repair before the failure. Pick a share of the remaining pool that you can defend, and write down the reasoning next to it: which assets will be monitored, which failure modes they cover, and why you chose that share instead of a higher one.


A conservative share that finance can check is worth more than an ambitious one they have to take on faith. If the real result turns out better, you've built credibility for the next request.


Multiply your avoidable events by the value per event from each benefit bucket, and you have the dollar value of the share you can avoid.


## What payback should you expect, and how do you present it?


Payback is how long the avoided cost takes to cover the cost of the fix: hardware, software, installation and your team's time. Present it as a range, so finance sees a floor and a best estimate.


For an outside reference, the[Verdantix Verified Value Delivery](https://tractian.com/en/resources/guides/verdantix-verified-value-delivery-study-financial-and-operational-assessment-of-tractian) study modeled a 401% ROI over three years and break-even in about 8 months. State the caveat plainly when you use it: those numbers come from a model of a mid-sized manufacturer ($200 million in revenue, 500 employees, 12 sites), validated through interviews with five Tractian customers. Use it to show that returns of this size are realistic, then let your own numbers set the forecast.


Show two scenarios in your own case, so finance sees a range instead of one figure:


- **Conservative case:** a low avoidable share, lower value per event, and only the production and labor-and-parts buckets. This is the version that has to clear the ROI threshold on its own.
- **Base case:** your best estimate of the avoidable share and value per event, with secondary damage included.


A range shows finance you've thought about what could go wrong and gives them a floor they can approve with confidence. If the conservative case pays back within the budget horizon, the decision gets much easier.


Finance may still want proof before they fund a full rollout. That's what a pilot is for: a defined set of assets, a clear baseline and a time frame long enough to see real catches.


## FAQ


**How long does predictive maintenance take to pay back?**


It depends on your exposure, the share you can avoid and the cost of the fix, which is why your case should show a conservative and a base scenario. As a reference point, the Verdantix Verified Value Delivery study modeled break-even in about 8 months for a mid-sized manufacturer. Use your own numbers to see where your plant falls.


**What if finance does not trust the savings numbers?**


Show your work. Separate the benefit buckets, state your assumptions and lead with the conservative case. If finance still wants proof, propose a pilot on a small set of critical assets with a clear baseline.
